arXiv:2602.15338v1 [cs.LG] 17 Feb 2026

Discovering Implicit Large Language Model Alignment Objectives

Edward Chen Affiliation: Stanford University Correspondence to: edjchen@cs.stanford.edu    Sanmi Koyejo Affiliation: Stanford University    Carlos Guestrin Affiliation: Stanford University
Abstract

Large language model (LLM) alignment relies on complex reward signals that often obscure the specific behaviors being incentivized, creating critical risks of misalignment and reward hacking. Existing interpretation methods typically rely on pre-defined rubrics, risking the omission of "unknown unknowns", or fail to identify objectives that comprehensively cover and are causal to the model behavior. To address these limitations, we introduce Obj-Disco, a framework that automatically decomposes an alignment reward signal into a sparse, weighted combination of human-interpretable natural language objectives. Our approach utilizes an iterative greedy algorithm to analyze behavioral changes across training checkpoints, identifying and validating candidate objectives that best explain the residual reward signal. Extensive evaluations across diverse tasks, model sizes, and alignment algorithms demonstrate the framework’s robustness. Experiments with popular open-source reward models show that the framework consistently captures > 90% of reward behavior, a finding further corroborated by human evaluation. Additionally, a case study on alignment with an open-source reward model reveals that Obj-Disco can successfully identify latent misaligned incentives that emerge alongside intended behaviors. Our work provides a crucial tool for uncovering the implicit objectives in LLM alignment, paving the way for more transparent and safer AI development.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences is a prerequisite for deploying safe and useful artificial intelligence (AI) systems. To scale this process beyond expensive human supervision, developers typically optimize models against complex proxy reward functions, such as learned reward models or LLM-as-a-Judge systems (Ouyang et al., 2022; Dann et al., 2023; Go et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Christian et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025b; Gunjal et al., 2025). While scalable, this abstraction creates a critical challenge: the complexity of these reward functions often renders the objectives embedded within them opaque, making it difficult to discern precisely what behaviors the model is being aligned towards. This ambiguity can create a divergence between the intended goals and the realized behaviors, leading models to adopt misaligned shortcuts such as sycophancy or verbosity (Tamkin et al., 2023; Singhal et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2023). Consequently, developing methods to break down and interpret the implicit objectives driving LLM alignment is essential for ensuring robust and trustworthy deployment.

While developers can attempt to infer implicit alignment objectives by observing the model’s behavioral evolution, relying on manual inspection is insufficient for capturing the full breadth of changes. Standard practice typically involves monitoring behavioral trends based on a predefined set of objectives on a static validation dataset (Stiennon et al., 2022; Dubois et al., 2024; Singhal et al., 2024). However, this paradigm is fundamentally constrained by two distinct coverage limitations. First, the static nature of the datasets inevitably biases the analysis, potentially missing unintended behaviors that only manifest on certain inputs. Second, even assuming comprehensive data oversight, humans face a significant cognitive bottleneck in enumerating objectives to attain coverage. Humans generally lack the capacity to track the subtle distributional shifts required to identify "unknown unknowns" across thousands of outputs (Ribeiro & Lundberg, 2022; Gao et al., 2023; Dunlap et al., 2024; Dunlap et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2025; Williams et al., 2025). Even when a potential objective is identified, validating its semantic meaning requires grounding it in concrete examples; without a curated set of illustrative trajectories, developers may struggle to interpret how an abstract objective like "helpfulness" actually materializes across different contexts. Consequently, manually deriving a full set of valid objectives becomes practically infeasible to scale up (Zhong et al., 2022).

To address these scalability challenges, recent research has introduced automated frameworks to help understand model behavior. However, these systems operate primarily as benchmarks constrained by predefined metrics. Unlike discovery-based approaches, the majority of these works are prescriptive and evaluate models using a fixed set of objectives (Pan et al., 2023; Murthy et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2024; Ryan et al., 2025). This inherently limits their ability to uncover unanticipated "unknown unknowns." Conversely, descriptive “proposer-validator” frameworks attempt to explain differences between datasets or models from a blank slate (Dunlap et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2022; Zhong et al., 2025; Dunlap et al., 2025). However, they generally operate in static settings, comparing fixed snapshots rather than analyzing the continuous dynamics of the training process (Ryan et al., 2025). Consequently, prior works fail to leverage a rich source of signal regarding what LLMs actually learn during alignment: the trajectory of model weights checkpointed during training. Without this temporal information, these methods struggle to disentangle the model’s pre-existing inductive biases from the specific behaviors actively reinforced by the reward signal. Our work bridges this gap by leveraging these checkpoints to facilitate higher-fidelity objective discovery without relying on predefined categories.

We introduce Obj-Disco, a framework that automatically decomposes an LLM’s implicit alignment objectives into a set of objectives expressed using natural language, which we refer to as the Discovered Interpretable Reward (DIR). Our approach rests on the core assumption that the reward signal driving alignment can be approximated as a function of separate basis functions, or objectives, as also pointed out by Silver et al (2021) (Jang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Go et al., 2024; Sharma et al., 2025). Accordingly, we frame this task as a sparse representation problem and employ an iterative, greedy algorithm inspired by matching pursuit to sequentially identify the objectives that best explain the residual reward signal (Mallat & Zhang, 1993). To ensure both coverage and validity, each iteration of Obj-Disco consists of a structured Objectives Discovery phase followed by an Objectives Verification phase. During discovery, we address the intractability of the exponential objective space by using a proposer LLM to generate candidates based on response trajectories observed across multiple training checkpoints. By dynamically sampling inputs where the residual error is largest, we explicitly guide the proposer to target unexplained behavioral shifts and select the candidate that minimizes this residual. Subsequently, the verification phase utilizes LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations to screen the selected candidate against formal criteria, ensuring it is both human-interpretable and follows a predictable trend throughout alignment fine-tuning. Finally, to aid developer understanding, Obj-Disco provides Objective Explanations, a curated set of sample trajectories selected to maximize both trend salience and semantic diversity, offering concrete evidence for each discovered objective.

We validate Obj-Disco through an extensive experimental suite spanning multiple alignment algorithms, model sizes, and tasks. In controlled settings with known ground-truth objectives, our framework recovers the target signals with high fidelity, consistently modeling over 90% of the true alignment behavior. Experiments on popular open-source reward models further demonstrate that Obj-Disco can approximate complex, implicit reward functions with similar accuracy. To verify the practical utility of these discoveries, we conduct human-subject studies which confirm that our DIRs are significantly more causal to the final policy behavior than those identified by baseline methods. Participants also rated our Objective Explanations as having higher fidelity to the underlying objective signals. Finally, a targeted case study on safety alignment reveals that Obj-Disco consistently successfully surfaces latent misaligned incentives, such as increased permissiveness in discussing illegal acts, which other baselines rarely detect.

2 Problem Definition

We consider the a posteriori setting, where an LLM has already been aligned. Specifically, we assume access to a full sequence of 𝒯\mathcal{T} model checkpoints, πθ1,…,πθ𝒯\pi_{\theta_{1}},\dots,\pi_{\theta_{\mathcal{T}}}, saved chronologically during an alignment process such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). Our goal is to analyze this alignment trajectory to discover the set of implicit objectives the model has learned. We make no assumptions about the characteristics of the checkpoint sequence.

We formally define an objective as a function rn:𝒳×𝒴→𝒪r_{n}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{O} which maps prompts in space 𝒳\mathcal{X} and responses in 𝒴\mathcal{Y} to a scalar score in 𝒪\mathcal{O}. For simplicity, we assume 𝒪=[0,1]\mathcal{O}=[0,1]. We posit that for an objective to be useful for human understanding, it must meet two key desiderata:

Desiderata 1: An objective is human-interpretable. An objective rr is human-interpretable if its scoring function can be closely approximated by the scores a (human) evaluator would assign based on its natural language description. Let sh​(x,y|n)∈𝒪s_{h}(x,y|n)\in\mathcal{O} denote the score a (human) evaluator assigns to the input-output pair, xx, yy, when using the natural language description nn. An objective rr is then human-interpretable if:

1𝒯∑t=1𝒯𝔼x∼𝒳,y∼πθt(⋅|x)[|rn(x,y)−sh(x,y|n)|]≤ϵi​n​t​e​r​p\dfrac{1}{\mathcal{T}}\sum_{t=1}^{\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{X},y\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot|x)}[|r_{n}(x,y)-s_{h}(x,y|n)|]\leq\epsilon_{interp} (1)

Desiderata 2: An objective follows a predictable trend. An objective rr follows a trend if the model’s performance on that objective, measured across the sequence of models, is predictable. Let Vnt​(r)V_{n}^{t}(r) denote the expected score of objective rr, with natural language description nn, with respect to model πθt\pi_{\theta_{t}}:

Vnt(r)=𝔼x∼X,y∼πθt(⋅|x)[rn(x,y)]V_{n}^{t}(r)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim X,y\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot|x)}[r_{n}(x,y)] (2)

The objective rr follows a predictable trend if the sequence of scores Vn1​(r),…,Vn𝒯​(r)V_{n}^{1}(r),...,V_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}(r) can be fit with a function from a pre-defined class ℱt​r​e​n​d\mathcal{F}_{trend} (e.g. linear function). Formally,

f∗=arg​minf∈ℱtrend1𝒯−1∑t=2𝒯ℒ(f(t|Vn1:t−1(r)),Vnt(r))f^{*}=\argmin_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{trend}}\dfrac{1}{\mathcal{T}-1}\sum_{t=2}^{\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{L}(f(t|V_{n}^{1:t-1}(r)),V_{n}^{t}(r)) (3)

where ℒ\mathcal{L} is a squared error loss function. We claim that the objective rr follows a predictable trend if the average prediction error is bounded:

1𝒯−1∑t=2𝒯ℒ(f∗(t|Vn1:t−1(r)),Vnt(r))≤ϵt​r​e​n​d\dfrac{1}{\mathcal{T}-1}\sum_{t=2}^{\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{L}(f^{*}(t|V_{n}^{1:t-1}(r)),V_{n}^{t}(r))\leq\epsilon_{trend} (4)

In practice, we operationalize rnr_{n} with an LLM-as-a-Judge setup, detailed in Appendix A.4 (Zheng et al., 2023). Overall, we assume there are kk implicit objectives, where kk is determined by the user. As a result, we aim to discover the underlying set of objectives R∗={rn1,…,rnk}R^{*}=\{r_{n_{1}},...,r_{n_{k}}\}.

2.1 Objectives Approximation

Given a sequence of models πθ1,…,πθ𝒯\pi_{\theta_{1}},\dots,\pi_{\theta_{\mathcal{T}}} from an alignment process on a target dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, our main goal is to uncover the Discovered Interpretable Reward (DIR), a set of interpretable objectives ℛ^\hat{\mathcal{R}} that explains the underlying reward signal ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*}. We assume this signal to be shaped by the interplay between the training data 𝒟\mathcal{D}, the alignment algorithm, and the final operating point among objectives (Wei et al., 2023; Lambert & Calandra, 2024; Guo et al., 2024). We hypothesize that the total reward can be decomposed into a simple function of our discovered objectives, allowing us to quantitatively measure how well ℛ^\hat{\mathcal{R}} approximates ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*}.

To formalize this, we use the standard RLHF setting with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) as a canonical example (Schulman et al., 2017). In this setup, the policy πθt\pi_{\theta_{t}} is optimized to maximize a reward r⁡(x,y)r(x,y) for prompts x∈𝒟x\in\mathcal{D}:

r⁡(x,y)=rϕ​(x,y)−β⁡(log⁡πθt​(y|x)−log⁡πr​e​f​(y|x))r(x,y)=r_{\phi}(x,y)-\beta(\log\pi_{\theta_{t}}(y|x)-\log\pi_{ref}(y|x)) (5)

rϕ​(x,y)r_{\phi}(x,y) is associated with a reward model trained on human preferences derived from the domain 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and it is this component that contains the implicit objectives we aim to discover. Our central hypothesis is that this complex reward model score can be approximated by a simple, low-complexity function 𝒞\mathcal{C}, which we refer to as the composition function11 1 See Sharma et al. (2025), Hosking et al. (2024), and Go et al. (2024) for evidence of human preferences being predicted with a function of interpretable features. (e.g., linear regression or gradient boosting), over our discovered set of objectives ℛ^\hat{\mathcal{R}}:

rϕ​(x,y)≈𝒞⁡(r^n1​(x,y),…,r^n|R^|​(x,y))r_{\phi}(x,y)\approx\mathcal{C}(\hat{r}_{n_{1}}(x,y),\dots,\hat{r}_{n_{|\hat{R}|}}(x,y)) (6)

Here, 𝒞\mathcal{C} primarily serves to learn the appropriate scaling and trade-offs (the operating point) between the discovered objectives in ℛ^\hat{\mathcal{R}}. To quantitatively measure how well R^\hat{R} approximates R∗R^{*}, we first define the pointwise squared residual as ℰ(x,y;R^)=(R∗(x,y)−𝒞(r^n1(x,y),…,r^n|R^|(x,y)))2\mathcal{E}(x,y;\hat{R})=(R^{*}(x,y)-\mathcal{C}(\hat{r}_{n_{1}}(x,y),...,\hat{r}_{n_{|}\hat{R}|}(x,y)))^{2}, where the dependency on R∗R^{*} is implicit. Following the PPO example above, R∗={r}R^{*}=\{r\}. We then define Obj-Error as the root-mean-square of these residuals averaged over the alignment trajectory:

Obj-Error ​(R^,R∗)=[1𝒯​∑t=1𝒯𝔼x,y∼πθt​[ℰ⁡(x,y,R^)]]1/2\text{Obj-Error }(\hat{R},R^{*})=\left[\dfrac{1}{\mathcal{T}}\sum_{t=1}^{\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}}\left[\mathcal{E}(x,y;\hat{R})\right]\right]^{1/2} (7)

Intuitively, a lower Obj-Error indicates that our discovered objectives provide a better fit for the ground-truth reward signal. The squared error term ℰ\mathcal{E} penalizes outliers that may point to unexplained aspects of the reward.

As a result, our main goal is to obtain:

R^=arg​minR^⊂ℛ,|R^|≤k⁡Obj-Error ​(R^,R∗)\hat{R}=\argmin_{\hat{R}\subset\mathcal{R},|\hat{R}|\leq k}\text{Obj-Error }(\hat{R},R^{*}) (8)

While we use PPO as our example here, Obj-Disco applies to any alignment algorithm with an explicit reward signal, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024). Additional details in Appendix A.2.

3 Proposed Method: Obj-Disco

Our method takes inspiration from the Matching Pursuit algorithm (Mallat & Zhang, 1993), which greedily builds up a sparse approximation of a signal. In our setting, the “signal” is the underlying reward function R∗R^{*} that guides the model’s alignment, and our goal is to approximate it with the function 𝒞\mathcal{C} over a small set of kk interpretable objectives R^\hat{R} (Equation 8). To solve this optimization problem, we propose an iterative greedy algorithm that, at each iteration ii, selects the single objective that provides the maximum marginal decrease in our objective error:

minrn∈ℛ⁡[Obj-Error ​(R^i−1∪{rn},R∗)−Obj-Error ​(R^i−1,R∗)]\min_{r_{n}\in\mathcal{R}}[\text{Obj-Error }(\hat{R}^{i-1}\cup\{r_{n}\},R^{*})-\text{Obj-Error }(\hat{R}^{i-1},R^{*})] (9)

where R^i−1\hat{R}^{i-1} is the set of estimated objectives from the previous iteration. Minimizing Equation 9 is equivalent to finding the objective rnr_{n} that best explains the current residuals, which corresponds to solving the following problem:

rn∗=arg​minrn∈ℛ⁡1𝒯​∑t=1𝒯𝔼x,y∼πθt​[ℰ⁡(x,y,R^i−1∪{rn})]r_{n}^{*}=\argmin_{r_{n}\in\mathcal{R}}\frac{1}{\mathcal{T}}\sum_{t=1}^{\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}}\left[\mathcal{E}(x,y;\hat{R}^{i-1}\cup\{r_{n}\})\right] (10)

Intuitively, this seeks the objective rn∗r_{n}^{*} that best approximates the unexplained differences between the true and predicted objectives.

Solving the above directly presents two significant challenges. First, a direct search for rn∗r_{n}^{*} over the discrete text space ℛ\mathcal{R} is hard. Second, verifying that a candidate objective rnr_{n} is valid requires ensuring it meets our desiderata from Section 2, namely being human-interpretable and following a predictable trend, which are non-trivial properties to assess. Our algorithm addresses these two challenges with a two-step process at each iteration ii:

1. Objectives Discovery. Searching over the discrete text space ℛ\mathcal{R} is hard. Section 3.1 addresses this by using a powerful “proposer” LLM to analyze model response trajectories and propose a small, high-quality set of candidate objectives Rcandi⊂ℛR^{i}_{\text{cand}}\subset\mathcal{R}. This process is guided by a principled, sampling-based strategy to select the most informative samples for the LLM to analyze.

2. Objectives Verification. Verifying the properties of human-interpretability and trend-predictability typically require human input, which is expensive. Section 3.2 instead leverages LLM-as-a-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023) to validate the best candidate from ℛcandi\mathcal{R}^{i}_{\text{cand}} against our desiderata. The algorithm concludes once |R^i|=k|\hat{R}^{i}|=k.

3.1 Step 1: Objectives Discovery

To efficiently search the discrete space ℛ\mathcal{R} for the next objective, we employ a proposer LLM to hypothesize candidates based on informative response trajectories. We structure this discovery process into three phases: identifying the most informative samples to analyze, using them to generate candidate objectives, and then greedily selecting the optimal candidate.

Informative Samples Identification. Equation 10 aims to identify the objective rnr_{n} that minimizes the residual error across the entire data distribution. To guide the discovery of such a generalizable objective, we direct the proposer’s attention toward regions of the input space where the current approximation is most deficient. Specifically, we seek a set of inputs that yields the highest average residual error. Maximizing the average ensures that the discovered objective addresses systematic behavioral trends unexplained by the current set R^i−1\hat{R}^{i-1}, rather than overfitting to isolated outliers. Given the finite context window of the proposer LLM, we constrain this discovery set 𝕏disc\mathbb{X}_{\text{disc}} to a fixed cardinality ν\nu. Formally, we seek to solve the following maximization:

𝕏disc=argmax𝕏⊂𝒳,|𝕏|=ν1𝒯​∑t=1𝒯𝔼x∼𝕏,y∼πθt​[ℰ⁡(x,y,R^i−1)]\mathbb{X}_{\text{disc}}=\operatorname*{argmax}_{\mathbb{X}\subset\mathcal{X},|\mathbb{X}|=\nu}\dfrac{1}{\mathcal{T}}\sum_{t=1}^{\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{X},y\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}}[\mathcal{E}(x,y;\hat{R}^{i-1})] (11)

Finding the exact solution to Equation 11 over the full dataset is computationally prohibitive. We therefore approximate this via a scalable two-stage process. First, we draw a larger random candidate pool 𝕏cand⊂𝒳\mathbb{X}_{\text{cand}}\subset\mathcal{X} of size NcandN_{\text{cand}}. This stochastic step avoids the cost of evaluating the entire input space while maintaining exploration coverage. Second, we compute the trajectory-averaged residuals for these candidates and select the top ν\nu instances to form 𝕏disc\mathbb{X}_{\text{disc}}.

Candidate Objectives Discovery. Using the identified set of informative samples 𝕏disc\mathbb{X}_{\text{disc}}, we then prompt the proposer LLM to generate our candidate objectives ℛcandi\mathcal{R}^{i}_{\text{cand}}. To have control over the granularity of discovered objectives, we split the set of ν\nu inputs in 𝕏disc\mathbb{X}_{\text{disc}} into batches of size bb and provide bb full response trajectories to the proposer LLM at a time. To encourage the discovery of novel and non-redundant axes, we provide the already-discovered objectives R^i−1\hat{R}^{i-1} as part of the prompt’s context. The proposer LLM is then prompted to describe the primary behavioral trend observed in the samples. The prompt we use is shown in Figure 7. The union of all unique natural language objectives proposed across the inputs forms our candidate objectives set ℛcandi\mathcal{R}^{i}_{\text{cand}}.

Objectives Selection. Finally, we identify the optimal objective rni,∗r_{n}^{i,*} from the candidate set ℛcandi\mathcal{R}^{i}_{\text{cand}} by solving Equation 9 restricted to these proposed candidates. The selected objective is then passed to the Objectives Verification stage.

3.2 Step 2: Objectives Verification

We now check the validity of the selected objective rni,∗r_{n}^{i,*} by determining whether it is human-interpretable and follows a predictable trend, as described in Section 2.

Human-Interpretability Verification. To ensure a robust and representative validation of human-interpretability, we compute the human-aligned score sh​(x,y|n)s_{h}(x,y|n) in Equation 1 by aggregating judgments from an ensemble of LLM-as-a-Judge models. This approach mitigates the idiosyncratic biases of any single model and captures a more generalizable consensus (Sun et al., 2025). Within the set of evaluator models, ℳe​v​a​l={m1,…,mℓ}\mathcal{M}_{eval}=\{m_{1},...,m_{\ell}\}, each evaluator mm is provided with a standardized scoring template, including the objective description nn, input xx, and response yy, and is instructed to output a numerical score. The final human-aligned score is computed as:

sh​(x,y|n)=1|ℳe​v​a​l|​∑m∈ℳe​v​a​lsm​(x,y|n)s_{h}(x,y|n)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}_{eval}|}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}_{eval}}s_{m}(x,y|n)

The objective is then deemed human-interpretable if Equation 1 is satisfied. Additional details in Appendix A.3.2.

Trend-Predictability Verification. To validate the criterion of trend-predictability, we analyze whether the objective’s expected scores across the model sequence follow a predictable pattern (Equation 4). We iteratively fit the sequence of scores {Vn1​(r),…,Vn𝒯​(r)}\{V_{n}^{1}(r),...,V_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}(r)\} to a predefined class of trend functions ℱtrend\mathcal{F}_{\text{trend}}. Following established literature on parametric learning curves (Viering & Loog, 2022), we populate ℱtrend\mathcal{F}_{\text{trend}} with functions that model common optimization behaviors, specifically: (1) linear growth, (2) logarithmic growth, (3) power law with an asymptote, and (4) exponential saturation. An objective is deemed valid if its trajectory can be fit by any function in ℱtrend\mathcal{F}_{\text{trend}} such that the error bound in Equation 4 is satisfied. While we employ these specific forms to capture standard learning behaviors, our framework is agnostic to the choice of ℱtrend\mathcal{F}_{\text{trend}} and can accommodate other function classes.

Finally, if both criteria are satisfied, we set R^i=R^i−1∪{rni,∗}\hat{R}^{i}=\hat{R}^{i-1}\cup\{r_{n}^{i,*}\}. If any of the criteria are not met, we proceed with R^i=R^i−1\hat{R}^{i}=\hat{R}^{i-1} and go to the next iteration. This ensures that only objectives that exhibit human-interpretability and trend-predictability are included in our final set of discovered objectives. Additional details in Appendix A.3.

3.3 Exemplar-Based Objective Explanations

To help users understand the behavior of a discovered objective rnr_{n}, Obj-Disco presents explanations in the form of a small set of input-response trajectory samples illustrative of that objective, which we refer to as Objective Explanations (or OEs). As manual inspection of the entire dataset would be cognitively prohibitive, our goal is to select a sparse subset of points that maintains as much explanatory utility as possible. We achieve this by leveraging the notion of diminishing returns: the marginal utility of adding a sample decreases if similar samples are already represented in the set. This notion is formally encapsulated by the property of submodularity, which allows us to design optimization algorithms with strong theoretical guarantees (Nemhauser et al., 1978) (Appendix A.3.3).

We construct the OE set EE based on two desiderata. First, Trend Fidelity: the selected samples must closely follow the global behavioral trend identified for rnr_{n}, ensuring the alignment effect is visually consistent. Second, Diversity: the samples must cover distinct semantic clusters of the input space (e.g., coding, creative writing) to demonstrate that the objective is a general behavioral principle rather than an artifact of a specific domain.

Formally, we define a sample trajectory ξ∈Ξ\xi\in\Xi as the tuple containing an input prompt xx and the sequence of model responses across the 𝒯\mathcal{T} checkpoints: ξ=(x,yπθ1,…,yπθ𝒯)\xi=(x,y_{\pi_{\theta_{1}}},\dots,y_{\pi_{\theta_{\mathcal{T}}}}). Given the set of all available trajectories Ξ\Xi, we aim to select a subset E⊂ΞE\subset\Xi subject to a cardinality constraint |E|≤κ|E|\leq\kappa, where κ\kappa is a small integer (e.g., 5) to ensure the OE remains manageable for human inspection.

Trend Fidelity: We quantify how well a specific sample trajectory ξ\xi exemplifies the global trend f∗​(t)f^{*}(t) (defined in Equation 3) by adapting Equation 4 and calculating the squared L2-error between the sample’s objective scores ut=rn​(ξx,ξyπθt)u_{t}=r_{n}(\xi_{x},\xi_{y_{\pi_{\theta_{t}}}}) and the global trend values. We convert this error into a similarity score using the following:

fid(ξ)=exp(−∑t=1𝒯(ut−f∗(t))2)\text{fid}(\xi)=\exp\left(-\sum_{t=1}^{\mathcal{T}}(u_{t}-f^{*}(t))^{2}\right) (12)

Following this, we define the total fidelity of the OE as a modular function: ffid​(E)=∑ξ∈Efid​(ξ)f_{\text{fid}}(E)=\sum_{\xi\in E}\text{fid}(\xi).

Diversity: To ensure semantic coverage, we first partition the input space Ξ\Xi into mm semantic clusters 𝒫={P1,…,Pm}\mathcal{P}=\{P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\} (e.g., via K-Means on prompt embeddings). We employ a diversity function explicitly designed to capture diminishing returns. Instead of simply counting samples, we sum the square roots of the counts of selected items per partition. Because the square root function is concave, the marginal gain of adding a sample from a specific cluster decreases as more samples from that cluster are added. This formulation is known to be monotone submodular (Prasad et al., 2014; Tschiatschek et al., 2014):

fdiv​(E)=∑j=1m|E∩Pj|f_{\text{div}}(E)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sqrt{|E\cap P_{j}|} (13)

The final objective is a convex combination parameterized by λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]: F⁡(E)=(1−λ)​ffid​(E)+λ​fdiv​(E)F(E)=(1-\lambda)f_{\text{fid}}(E)+\lambda f_{\text{div}}(E). Since the property of submodularity is closed under convex combinations, the total objective F⁡(E)F(E) is monotone submodular. Consequently, maximizing F⁡(E)F(E) under a cardinality constraint can be solved using the standard greedy algorithm (Algorithm 1) with a theoretical guarantee of achieving at least (1−1/e)(1-1/e) of the optimal solution (Nemhauser et al., 1978). Additional details in Appendix A.3.3.

4 Experimental Setup

We comprehensively validate the efficacy of Obj-Disco by first assessing reconstruction fidelity with a controlled synthetic environment where ground-truth objectives are explicitly known. Second, we demonstrate real-world applicability by decomposing the implicit signals of popular open-source reward models, including DeBERTaV3 and the Skywork Reward family, across varied policy models and alignment algorithms. To rigorously verify our findings, we conduct two user studies evaluating the causal impact of our discovered rewards and the fidelity of the generated Objective Explanations. Finally, we perform extensive ablations to isolate the contributions of key components of our algorithm.

4.1 Setup Details

We evaluate on two open-source LLMs of different families: Llama-3.1-8B (meta llama, ) and Qwen3-4B (Team, 2025). We perform alignment using two different RLHF algorithms: PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) and GRPO (Shao et al., 2024).

Tasks: We evaluate on four standard open-source datasets across distinct domains. Summarization: Reddit TL;DR dataset (TLDR) from Stiennon et al. (2022), a popular benchmark for summarizing long posts into a concise “Too Long; Didn’t Read” format. Multi-Turn Dialogue: Anthropic Helpful and Harmless (HH-RLHF) dataset (Bai et al., 2022), which contains conversational dialogues involving anything from astrophysics to relationship advice. Instruction-Following: 10k prompt instances from GPT4-Alpaca, which uses GPT-4 (OpenAI et al., 2024) to generate output answers using the same prompt instances as the Stanford Alpaca dataset (Taori et al., 2023). Diverse Domains (Math/Coding/Safety): Skywork-Reward dataset (Sky), which consists of 80k prompts from a diverse array of domains such as math, coding, safety, information seeking, and data analysis (Liu et al., 2024).

Baseline Methods. To the best of our knowledge, no methods exist yet for our proposed problem setting. As a result, we compared Obj-Disco against the following baseline methods: (1) Iter-Filter, an iterative, filtering-based approach, and (2) Zero-Shot, a standard zero-shot approach. Iter-Filter is inspired by the algorithm from VibeCheck (Dunlap et al., 2025) and IterAlign (Chen et al., 2024). We generate a set of objectives at once, filter out the ones which do not satisfy the two criteria, and then iteratively do that until we obtain kk objectives. Zero-Shot serves to represent a simple discovery-based baseline; obtain a random sample and hypothesize a set of kk objectives based on their trajectories. More details about the baselines in Appendix A.4.

4.2 Evaluation Of Discovered Objectives

We aim to evaluate the functional utility of the discovered objectives R^\hat{R} for the downstream task of alignment. Specifically, if R^\hat{R} accurately captures the implicit incentives of the ground-truth reward R∗R^{*}, a policy optimized against R^\hat{R} should converge to a similar behavioral profile as one trained on R∗R^{*}. We operationalize this with the Model-Fit metric:

Model-Fit​(R^,t)=𝔼x∼𝒳,y∼πθ^t|R^​[R∗​(x,y)]𝔼x∼𝒳,y∼πθT|R∗​[R∗​(x,y)]\text{Model-Fit}(\hat{R},t)=\dfrac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{X},y\sim\pi_{\hat{\theta}_{t}|\hat{R}}}[R^{*}(x,y)]}{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{X},y\sim\pi_{\theta_{T}|R^{*}}}[R^{*}(x,y)]} (14)

where πθ^t|R^\pi_{\hat{\theta}_{t}|\hat{R}} is the policy model aligned with our DIR R^\hat{R} and πθT|R∗\pi_{\theta_{T}|R^{*}} is the policy model aligned with the true reward R∗R^{*}. A Model-Fit score approaching 1.0 indicates that R^\hat{R} successfully replicates the alignment signal of R∗R^{*}. We note that Model-Fit may sometimes exceed the value of 1 due to variance or the magnitude of the discovered objectives. We decided not to penalize this since it suggests that R^\hat{R} is a strong proxy for R∗R^{*}, potentially more effective at exhibiting the ground-truth reward signal.

5 Experimental Results

5.1 Controlled And Open-Source Reward Models

We construct a controlled alignment process where the ground-truth reward signal, ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*}, is defined as a linear combination of a pre-defined set of three LLM-as-a-Judge natural language objectives. This allows us to directly measure how faithfully Obj-Disco can recover these objectives. The specific objectives used are directly inspired by objectives used in OpenAI (2024); Bai et al. (2022); Glaese et al. (2022), are tailored to each task, and are detailed in Appendix A.5.2.

We also perform experiments using open-source reward models (RMs), notably reward-model-deberta-v3-large-v2 (DeRM) and Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.2-3B (SkyRM). For both, we vary across Llama-8B and Qwen-4B for the policy model. We use HH-RLHF and TLDR for DeRM and Skywork preference dataset for SkyRM (Liu et al., 2024). For Alpaca, we trained our own RM on a single dimension of a multi-objective preference dataset (Jang et al., 2023).

Results are shown in Figure 3. Open-source reward model qualitative results are shown in Figure 2. In all experimental settings, Obj-Disco was the only method to consistently surpass a Model-Fit of 90%, while often achieving higher scores than both Iter-Filter and Zero-Shot. Zero-Shot sometimes approaches the performance of Obj-Disco, albeit at a notably higher variance. One notable limitation of Zero-Shot is how it’s limited by the context-length or capabilities of the proposer LLM, which may be consequential in resource-constrained settings. We qualitatively illustrate the effects of this in Section 5.2. Additional results in Appendix A.5.

5.2 Case Study: Detecting Latent Misalignment

To demonstrate Obj-Disco’s utility in safety auditing, we analyze a real-world scenario prone to unintended behavioral shifts: multi-turn dialogue aligned towards helpfulness. To do this, we used GRPO with the open-source gpt2-large-helpful-reward-model. Although designed to promote general helpfulness, this reward model can inadvertently incentivize negative behaviors, i.e. sycophancy. We compare the discovered objectives of four baselines: (1) Iter-Filter, (2) Zero-Shot, (3) a Fixed-α\alpha variant restricted to a set of α\alpha pre-defined objectives, testing the value of open-ended search; and (4) Limited-Zero-Shot, which uses a restricted context window to simulate resource-constrained environments where analyzing large trajectory sets is infeasible.

The resulting objectives are presented in Figure 4. Notably, Obj-Disco was the only framework to consistently surface latent misaligned behaviors, such as “increase permissiveness in discussing illegal or unethical acts", in 3 out of 4 trials. The baselines surfaced misalignment in, at most, 1 out of 4 trials. This result underscores the fragility of Zero-Shot methods and highlights the robustness of our residual-driven selection strategy for uncovering subtle safety risks. Further details are provided in Appendix A.4.1 and A.5.1.

5.3 Objective Explanations Human-Subject Evaluation

We conducted a user study to validate the utility of our Objective Explanations (OEs) component for human end-users. Our central hypothesis posits that OEs provide representative trajectories that allow users to accurately identify the underlying objective. Participants were presented with sample response trajectories generated by either Obj-Disco or a random baseline and tasked with selecting the correct objective from a set of four possible ones (including distractors). We report the accuracy of identifying the true objective: Obj-Disco achieved an accuracy of 39.9% ±\pm 6.5%, significantly outperforming the random baseline (25.5% ±\pm 5.8%). A one-tailed binomial test against chance (25%) confirms the statistical significance of our method (p<0.001p<0.001), whereas the baseline showed no significant deviation (p=0.462p=0.462), demonstrating the superior explanatory power of our approach. Further details are provided in Appendix A.4.2.

5.4 Objectives Causality Human-Subject Evaluation

We conducted a user study to validate the core capability of Obj-Disco: identifying the implicit objectives that causally drive policy behavior. Our goal was to determine if a policy model trained on our Discovered Interpretable Reward (DIR) exhibits behaviors indistinguishable from those of the original aligned model. Participants were presented with a target response generated by the final checkpoint of the original aligned model and were asked to select the most behaviorally similar response from models aligned with the DIRs from Obj-Disco and baseline methods. Therefore, a higher selection frequency for Obj-Disco would indicate that its DIRs more accurately capture the causal drivers of the original aligned behavior. We report selection frequencies: Obj-Disco (35.6% ±\pm 4.3%), Iter-Filter (16.7% ±\pm 3.3%), Zero-Shot (27.1% ±\pm 4.0%), and base model (20.6% ±\pm 3.6%). A chi-square test rejected uniform selection (p<0.001p<0.001). Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons confirmed that Obj-Disco was preferred over Iter-Filter (p<0.001p<0.001), Zero-Shot (p<0.010p<0.010), and the base model (p<0.001p<0.001), indicating that Obj-Disco’s discovered objectives better reproduce the causal behavioral patterns of alignment. Further details are provided in Appendix A.4.3.

5.5 Ablation: Importance of Model Trajectory

A major differentiator of Obj-Disco from related works is that we leverage a trajectory of multiple model checkpoints for discovering objectives which are causal to the behaviors. We attempt to illustrate the importance of leveraging the full trajectory here. To do so, we obtain both quantitative and qualitative results for a variation of Obj-Disco which only uses the base model and final model checkpoint for discovery, which we refer to as Obj-Disco-Static. We obtain quantitative results using the controlled evaluation setting: HH-RLHF, GRPO, Llama-8B. The results are shown in Figure 5. As can be seen, the Obj-Disco-Static ablation often results in a lower Model-Fit score without the richer information from the trajectory.

We also evaluate this within the misalignment case study scenario due to its real world applicability We show the qualitative results in Figure 6. As can be seen, the DIRs from Obj-Disco-Static capture critical misaligned behaviors in only one out of four trials. Obj-Disco, on the other hand, does so in three out of four trials. Additionally, the DIRs from Obj-Disco-Static seem to often be correlated, or similar, to each other, resulting in decreased variety. Collectively, these findings suggest that the intermediate checkpoint trajectory provides a richer signal than what can be captured by static endpoints alone.

We also conduct extensive ablation studies over the composition function, Obj-Disco parameters, informative sampling and discovery process components. Results in Appendix A.5.1.

6 Related Works

LLM Evaluation. More recent research is specifically auditing the alignment of LLMs. Some works audit for value alignment by analyzing model responses on interactive benchmarks and specialized datasets (Ye et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Murthy et al., 2025; Hendrycks et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025a; Pan et al., 2023). In a study on the feasibility of auditing, Marks et al. first induced a hidden objective into a model and then tasked separate teams with discovering it using interpretability and prompting tools (2025). While insightful, these approaches typically rely on evaluating models against a pre-defined set of values or find a single, known hidden objective. Our work does not make such assumptions as developers often cannot anticipate the full range of behaviors that may emerge during alignment.

Understanding LLM Misalignment. A significant body of research focuses on understanding misalignment (Betley et al., 2025; Entezami & Naseh, 2025; Liang et al., 2023). Many studies have cataloged such unintended consequences, such as producing overly long responses (Singhal et al., 2024), reducing output diversity (Kirk et al., 2024), degrading refusal behavior (Song et al., 2025), and misleading humans or giving malicious advice (Wen et al., 2024; Betley et al., 2025; Ghandeharioun et al., 2024; Tamkin et al., 2023; MacDiarmid et al., 2025). Other works have proposed to mitigate certain misalignment through techniques like causal reward modeling (Wang et al., 2025), balanced preference datasets (Singhal et al., 2024), or decoupling reward from confounding variables (Shen et al., 2023). Our work instead focuses on discovery from scratch rather than mitigation or documentation of a bias.

Reward Model Interpretability. Jiang et al. leverage controlled perturbations to interpret RMs and propose to generate contrastive explanations by modifying responses along a predefined set of attributes (e.g., helpfulness, verbosity) and observing the impact on the RM’s preference (2025b). Christian et al. perform an exhaustive search over the RM’s vocabulary, identifying tokens that are considered most "optimal" and "pessimal" to reveal any inherent biases (2025). Others have focused on decomposing a scalar reward into a multi-objective vector, making the trade-offs more explicit (Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). Finally, Marks et al. applied sparse autoencoders to interpret implicit RMs by analyzing features obtained from the activations between the base and fine-tuned model (2023). Instead of analyzing predefined, potentially correlated attributes, we discover objectives from scratch and aim to isolate out the directional nature of alignment and maximize coverage. Additional related works in Appendix A.1.

7 Conclusion

We introduced Obj-Disco, a framework which decomposes an opaque alignment reward signal into a set of interpretable natural language objectives. To do so, we employ an iterative greedy algorithm that analyzes the model’s behavioral trajectory, sequentially identifying and verifying the objectives that best explain the residual reward signal. Our extensive empirical evaluations confirm the method’s efficacy: in controlled settings with known objectives and with popular open-source reward models, Obj-Disco consistently recovers over 90% of the reward behavior, a finding strongly corroborated by human user studies and a case study identifying latent misalignment. Primary limitations include computational cost and reliance on LLM-based judges, which may introduce inherent biases (Zheng et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2025) (limitations in Appendix A.7). We believe Obj-Disco to be a step toward scalable, yet transparent, AI alignment. Future work may include extending this framework into an online and real-time setting.

Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work which may result from better understanding the behavior of the policy model after RL fine-tuning. We hope that our work may pave the path for safer and more transparent AI deployments by making more transparent any potential AI misalignment, biases, or other harmful behaviors.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Additional Related Works

LLM Evaluation. Evaluating the capabilities and behaviors of large language models (LLMs) has been a major focus of the natural language processing (NLP) community. Early efforts sought to improve upon classic metrics like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) and ROUGE (Lin, 2004) by developing more nuanced criteria for open-domain generation, such as fluency and conciseness (Pang et al., 2020; Sellam et al., 2020; Banerjee & Lavie, 2005). This has evolved into comprehensive benchmarking suites that measure model performance across a diverse set of pre-defined tasks and metrics (Liang et al., 2023; Srivastava et al., 2023; Kiela et al., 2021). To assess qualities like helpfulness and clarity without a ground-truth, others have leveraged LLMs themselves as scalable judges of model outputs (Mehri & Eskenazi, 2020a; Li et al., 2019; Mehri & Eskenazi, 2020b).

Automated Data Analysis. Automating the discovery of patterns in unstructured data is a long-standing goal, with classical methods like topic models aiming to extract topical variations from documents (Blei, 2012). More recently, a prominent line of work has leveraged LLMs to automatically propose and validate interpretable, natural language descriptions of differences between two static sets of data, such as texts or images (Zhong et al., 2022; Dunlap et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2025; Torii et al., 2024; Byun et al., 2023; Kahng et al., 2024). This includes systems like VibeCheck, which discovers qualitative differences to explain pairwise model preferences (Dunlap et al., 2025). More recently, StringSight is a tool using similar approaches to automate our understanding of agentic AI systems by analyzing their outputs (Dunlap, 2025). Report Cards is another work proposing to use LLMs to automatically generate human-interpretable, natural language summaries of language models, in the form of report cards (Yang et al., 2024). Ryan et al. focuses on the related task of interpreting human feedback with a set of correlated metrics (2025) but assumes a predefined initial set of metrics and a static feedback dataset. Our work is inspired by this paradigm of automated, language-based data analysis but makes several crucial departures. First, rather than comparing two (or more) distinct models or static datasets, we analyze the temporal evolution of a single model across its alignment trajectory. Second, our method does not rely on pairwise preference data or an initial set of predefined metrics as required by VibeCheck and AutoMetrics (Dunlap et al., 2025; Ryan et al., 2025); instead, it operates directly on the underlying reward signal. Finally, our framework generalizes beyond discovering binary predicates (e.g. (Zhong et al., 2025)) by aiming to identify any valid objective that exhibits a predictable trend, and we introduce a novel, principled sampling strategy based on alignment residuals to guide the discovery process.

Interpretable LLM Alignment Frameworks. While many alignment methods treat an LLM’s values as an implicit byproduct of training data, a distinct paradigm focuses on codifying desired behaviors into explicit, interpretable documents (Ouyang et al., 2022). These approaches, often called “Model Specifications” or “Constitutions”, provide a transparent foundation for alignment. Prominent examples include OpenAI’s Model Spec (OpenAI, 2024), Anthropic’s Constitutional AI (CAI) (Bai et al., 2022), and DeepMind’s Sparrow, which used a set of 23 natural-language rules (Glaese et al., 2022). This concept has been extended to democratically-sourced constitutions (Huang et al., 2024) and multi-objective alignment techniques that integrate a transparent set of goals into the model (Go et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024). Some work, like IterAlign (Chen et al., 2024), even aims to automatically discover a constitution from model behavior to improve alignment. Our work complements these prescriptive approaches; rather than defining a constitution for the model to follow, we aim to discover the implicit objectives a model has already learned from its alignment process.

Mechanistic Interpretability. Mechanistic interpretability is a bottom-up approach to interpretability which aims to study the fundamental components of models through fine-grained analysis of layers, neurons, and connections. The goal is often to uncover causal relationships transforming inputs to outputs, essential for fostering trust and transparency. Elhage et al. developed a mathematical framework to analyze up to a two layer attention-only transformer (2021). Foote et al. and Bills et al. proposed to leverage a larger language model to predict what a neuron in the smaller model represents (2023; 2023). Rather than study neurons as the fundamental unit, Black et al. proposed to study polytopes as the fundamental building block instead (2022). Bereska & Gavves provide a comprehensive survey on mechanistic interpretability approaches for AI safety (2024). Rather than study the internal mechanisms of the language models, our proposed method directly uses the model output behavioral changes to discover and quantify a set of interpretable objectives.

Exemplar-Based Explanations. One paradigm for enhancing the transparency of complex machine learning models is the use of exemplar-based explanations, which ground model decisions in specific, representative data instances rather than abstract feature scores (Wei et al., 2025; Hoang-Xuan et al., 2024). Concretely, prototype-based methods, originally developed for computer vision, aim to improve explainability by comparing inputs with representative examples rather than using abstract feature weights (Chen et al., 2019). For LLMs, Wei et al. developed a prototype-based model to explain the predictions of an LLM in a post-hoc manner (2025). Purohit et al. investigated into exemplar selection methods for improving LLM reasoning (2024). As users often desire for the sets of exemplars to be manageable in size, other works have applied submodular optimization to select such subsets, leveraging the property of diminishing returns to balance representativeness and semantic diversity (Tschiatschek et al., 2014; Sinha et al., 2011). Our work extends this paradigm by applying it to the temporal dimension of LLM alignment, using trajectory-based exemplars to explain the directional behavioral shifts actively reinforced during the alignment process.

A.2 Problem Definition

If the output scores for the rewards are normalized to be in [0, 1], as detailed in Section 2, then the square root in Equation 7 acts to push higher (or make worse) the Obj-Error scores for a worse set of R^\hat{R}.

In practice, to ensure a rigorous evaluation and to avoid overfitting, we calculate Obj-Error using a chronological train-test split across the model checkpoints. We designate the first set of models, from checkpoint 1 to 𝒯split\mathcal{T}_{\text{split}}, as the training set, and the subsequent models as the test set. The function 𝒞\mathcal{C} is fit exclusively on the training set; we learn its parameters by regressing the scores of our discovered objectives against the ground-truth reward scores for the early-stage model responses. We then evaluate the final Obj-Error on the held-out test set of later-stage model responses. This chronological split ensures we are measuring how well the objective relationships learned early in alignment generalize to the model’s behavior trajectory. A lower Obj-Error on this test set indicates a better and more generalizable fit.

When linear regression is used as the composition function 𝒞\mathcal{C}, we enforce positive coefficients as our discovery method assumes increasing trends across the checkpoints. Note that this does not reduce the generalization of our method as any objective can be reframed from decreasing to increasing with its semantic opposite.

A.3 Proposed Method

A.3.1 Objectives Discovery

Candidate Objectives Discovery. The prompt template used for objectives discovery is shown in Figure 7.

Objectives Selection. To ensure the selected objective generalizes to the model’s future behavior, we employ a chronological evaluation strategy: the composition function 𝒞\mathcal{C} is fitted on the initial training checkpoints (1​…​𝒯split1\dots\mathcal{T}_{\text{split}}), while the final selection is determined by minimizing the Obj-Error on the held-out test interval (𝒯split+1​…​𝒯\mathcal{T}_{\text{split}+1}\dots\mathcal{T}).

A.3.2 Objectives Verification

Trend-Predictability Verification. To operationalize the trend-predictability criterion, we define ℱtrend\mathcal{F}_{\text{trend}} as a library of parametric functions widely established in the learning curve literature for modeling performance trajectories (Viering & Loog, 2022). We specifically include models that capture distinct optimization dynamics, ranging from heavy-tailed improvement to rapid saturation:

  1. 1.

    Linear Growth: f⁡(t)=a​t+bf(t)=at+b. Represents strictly increasing, constant-rate improvement.

  2. 2.

    Logarithmic Growth: f⁡(t)=a​ln⁡(t)+bf(t)=a\ln(t)+b. Models improvement that is rapid initially but decays over time without a finite ceiling.

  3. 3.

    Power Law with Asymptote: f⁡(t)=c−a​t−bf(t)=c-at^{-b}. Frequently observed in LLM scaling laws, this models "heavy tail" learning that approaches an asymptotic limit cc as t→∞t\to\infty.

  4. 4.

    Exponential Saturation: f⁡(t)=S+g⁡(1−e−k⁡(t−1))f(t)=S+g(1-e^{-k(t-1)}). Models rapid initial learning that quickly converges to a performance ceiling, where SS is the starting score, gg is the total possible gain, and kk is the convergence rate.

We emphasize that while we employ these specific forms to capture standard learning behaviors, Obj-Disco is theoretically agnostic to the contents of ℱtrend\mathcal{F}_{\text{trend}} and can accommodate any user-defined class of trend functions.

A.3.3 Exemplar-Based Objective Explanations

The construction of Objective Explanations (OEs) for each discovered objective involves selecting a small, representative set of trajectory samples that maximize both trend fidelity and semantic diversity. To assist with computational tractability and financial cost, we first randomly sample 100 prompts from the dataset. Algorithm 1 then operates over those samples. We set the number of examples to κ=8\kappa=8 to ensure the summary remains manageable for human inspection while providing sufficient coverage. To balance the two desiderata, we set the fidelity-diversity trade-off parameter λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 in our objective function. For diversity calculations, we partition the input space into m=8m=8 semantic clusters using K-Means on embeddings generated by OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, where the input text for each embedding is formed by concatenating the prompt with its corresponding sequence of model responses.

(Nemhauser et al., 1978) In the case of any normalized, monotonic submodular function FF, the set EGE_{G} obtained by the greedy algorithm achieves at least a constant fraction (1−1e)(1-\dfrac{1}{e}) of the objective value obtained by the optimal solution, that is,

A.4 Experimental Setup

Scoring and Evaluation

For all experiments, unless otherwise noted, we utilize gpt-4o-mini as the LLM-as-a-Judge for evaluating objective scores (rnr_{n}). To ensure robust and calibrated scoring, we employ a dynamic prompting strategy. For each objective to be scored, the system first retrieves a domain-specific scoring rubric (e.g., specific criteria for "Helpfulness" in coding tasks vs. general dialogue) and a set of few-shot calibration examples (Low, Medium, and High scoring responses). If a predefined rubric or example set does not exist for a newly discovered objective, an auxiliary LLM call is made to generate them dynamically before scoring proceeds. The prompt templates used for scoring, rubric generation, and calibration examples generation are provided in Figures 8, 10, and 9, respectively. The prompt template used for objective discovery is provided in Figure 7.

To compute the human-interpretability verification (Section 3.2), we use gpt-4o-mini and gpt-4.1-nano for ℳe​v​a​l\mathcal{M}_{eval} and use 50 random samples. To compute trend-predictability, we used gpt-4o-mini for scoring and 50 random samples for Equation 2.

We compute the Model-Fit metric (Section 4.2) by randomly sampling two sets of 100 input samples from the test set of each of the tasks. Each model checkpoint is then passed through both sets of samples to compute the mean and standard error statistics.

Obj-Disco Parameters

Unless explicitly specified (e.g. for the ablations), we use the following parameters for Obj-Disco:

  • •

    Candidate Generation: We sample Ncand=100N_{\text{cand}}=100 candidate prompts and select the top ν=25\nu=25 most informative samples (based on residual error) for the discovery set 𝕏disc\mathbb{X}_{\text{disc}}.

  • •

    Proposer Configuration: We use GPT-4o-mini as the proposer model. For each batch of 3 trajectories, we generate 2 candidate objectives.

  • •

    Combination Function: We use linear regression to model the composition function 𝒞\mathcal{C}, fitting the weights of the discovered objectives to the ground-truth reward signal.

  • •

    Verification Thresholds: We set the threshold for interpretability ϵinterp=0.15\epsilon_{\text{interp}}=0.15 and for trend predictability ϵtrend=0.12\epsilon_{\text{trend}}=0.12.

To calculate Obj-Error, we set 𝒯split\mathcal{T}_{\text{split}} to 𝒯−1\mathcal{T}-1, meaning the final checkpoint is reserved as the held-out test set for evaluation. The specific checkpoint indices vary by experiment type to accommodate different convergence rates. For synthetic PPO experiments, we sample checkpoints at steps [0,25,50,75,100][0,25,50,75,100]. For PPO experiments using real reward models, we sample at [0,100,200,300][0,100,200,300], with the exception of the Alpaca dataset which uses [0,75,150,225][0,75,150,225] due to dataset constraints. For synthetic GRPO experiments, we use checkpoints [0,100,200,300][0,100,200,300], while GRPO experiments with open-source reward models are sampled at [0,125,250,375,500][0,125,250,375,500].

The weights for all discovered objectives from all compared methods are calculated from a final calculation of Obj-Error with 100 randomly sampled inputs at the end of the method.

Alignment Hyperparameters

For our validation experiments, we align models using both PPO and GRPO using the TRL library. The specific hyperparameters used are detailed below.

Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO): For training stability during RLHF on the policy model with open-source reward models, we modified the initial KL coefficient to be 0.05 and used 50 steps of linear learning rate warmup. Also for training stability purposes, for our empirical validation experiments, we kept the 50 steps of linear learning rate warmup, did not use score scaling and normalization, and used gpt-4.1-mini for scoring the rewards. For fair comparison, this set of parameters was kept the same across the different baseline discovery methods. For the other experimental settings, we followed those shown in Table 1.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO): Table 2.

Baseline Comparisons

Iter-Filter Details. Although VibeCheck (Dunlap et al., 2024) was designed for comparing two singular checkpoints of different model families, we took inspiration from it and used it as a baseline comparison. To initiate Iter-Filter, a random set of ν\nu inputs are sampled to form 𝕏disc\mathbb{X}_{\text{disc}}. As in VibeCheck (and Obj-Disco), we split the set of ν\nu inputs in 𝕏disc\mathbb{X}_{\text{disc}} into batches of size bb and provide bb full response trajectories to the proposer LLM at a time. The prompt we use for discovery is the same as the one used for Obj-Disco. We then randomly select objectives from the candidate set of objectives and check for human-interpretability and trend-predictability. The objectives which fail any of the criteria are filtered out of the set. If we end up with kk objectives after the filtering, then Iter-Filter concludes. Otherwise, we move on to the next iteration of Iter-Filter but instead focus discovery in the input samples in 𝕏disc\mathbb{X}_{\text{disc}} with the highest residuals (as also similarly done in VibeCheck).

Zero-Shot Details. The discovery prompt for Zero-Shot is instructed to output exactly kk objectives. Otherwise, the discovery prompt used is the same one as in Obj-Disco.

We ran 3 trials for each of our experiments. To ensure fair comparisons with baseline methods (Iter-Filter and Zero-Shot), we maintained consistent compute budgets and model configurations:

  • •

    Iter-Filter: We sample 25 random prompts per iteration (matching the size of 𝕏disc\mathbb{X}_{\text{disc}}) and use the same verification thresholds (ϵ=0.15/0.12\epsilon=0.15/0.12). 2 objectives are generated for each response trajectory in the set.

  • •

    Zero-Shot: This zero-shot approach uses a sample of 25 prompts (matching the size of 𝕏disc\mathbb{X}_{\text{disc}}) to propose objectives.

A.4.1 Detecting Latent Misalignment Case Study Setup

For our misalignment case study, we utilized the harmless-base subset of the Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset. We obtained the reward model from Hugging Face under the following tag: Ray2333/gpt2-large-helpful-reward_model. We supervise fine-tuned a Qwen3-4B base model using the HH-RLHF dataset, followed by GRPO for alignment. For this experiment only, we used gpt-4.1-mini as the proposer LLM across all comparisons.

In addition to Iter-Filter and Zero-Shot, we compared Obj-Disco against two specific ablation baselines. First, to demonstrate the value of our open-ended discovery setup, we compare against Fixed-α\alpha, a variation of Obj-Disco where, rather than using discovery to search over the entire space of objectives, the Objectives Selection component is done over a smaller, fixed set of α\alpha pre-defined objectives. Specifically we use α=3\alpha=3 and α=15\alpha=15. To generate the pre-defined list, we followed what a LLM model developer might currently do and sampled b=3b=3 inputs at each iteration, proposed 2 objectives for that batch, filtered out the ones which do not satisfy human-interpretability and trend predictability, and then repeated until we obtained 20 objectives.

Second, to highlight performance in resource-constrained settings, we compared against a Limited-Zero-Shot baseline, which used a reduced sample size of b=3b=3. We manually inspected samples from the final model checkpoint to ground-truth the presence of the misaligned behaviors identified by Obj-Disco.

A.4.2 Objective Explanations Human-Subject Evaluation Setup

We recruited 20 participants via Amazon Mechanical Turk for our human evaluation of the Objective Explanations component. We built the human-subject study application using Streamlit (str, 2018) and stored the data using Supabase (sup, 2020). Each participant completed a series of multiple-choice tasks designed to test the interpretability of the generated explanations. In each trial, the participant was presented with a set of four input-response trajectories. These trajectories were selected either by our proposed Objective Explanations algorithm (which optimizes for trend fidelity and diversity) or by a random baseline that samples four trajectories uniformly from the dataset.

Alongside the trajectories, participants were shown four potential objective descriptions: one correct ground-truth objective and three plausible distractor objectives. The distractor objectives were generated from gpt-4o-mini provided with the same response trajectories and using the prompt shown in Figure 11. The task was to identify which objective best described the behavioral trend observed in the trajectories. We collected a total of N=400N=400 judgments, split evenly between the two methods. Statistical significance was determined using a one-tailed binomial test with a theoretical random probability of success equal to 0.25 (1 out of 4 options).

Figures of the study are shown in Figures 12, 13, 14, 15.

A.4.3 Objectives Causality User Study Setup

We recruited 16 participants via Amazon Mechanical Turk for our human evaluation of objective causality. The study interface was developed using Streamlit, with response data securely stored and managed via Supabase. We collected a total of N=480N=480 judgments. For this evaluation, we focused specifically on experiments involving open-source reward models aligned via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Inputs were randomly sampled from the corresponding evaluation datasets to ensure diverse coverage. In each trial, participants were shown a prompt and a "reference response" generated by the fully aligned model. They were then presented with four anonymized candidate responses generated by: (1) a policy trained on the objectives discovered by Obj-Disco, (2) a policy trained on Iter-Filter objectives, (3) a policy trained on Zero-Shot objectives, and (4) the unaligned base model. Participants were instructed to select the candidate response that best matched the style, tone, and content of the reference response.

Figures of the study are shown in Figure 16, 17, 18, 19.

A.5 Additional Experimental Results

A.5.1 Ablation Studies

Unless otherwise noted, we run our ablation experiments with the following setting: GRPO, Llama-8B, the multi-turn HH-RLHF dataset, and the controlled ground-truth setting.

Ablation 1: Composition Function 𝒞\mathcal{C}. As described in Section 2, we use a simple, low-complexity model to scalarize the set of predicted objectives R^\hat{R}. We perform ablations over 𝒞\mathcal{C} using gradient boosting regression, linear regression, and a simple multi-layer perceptron (MLP). The results are shown in Figure 20. Overall, we observed similar Model-Fit trajectories and scores for all combinations. We used linear regression for the rest of our experiments for its simplicity and benefits of interpretability.

Ablation 2: Number of Parallel Trajectories for Candidate Objectives Discovery bb. As described in Section 3.1, the set of ν\nu inputs in 𝕏disc\mathbb{X}_{\text{disc}} is split into batches of size bb for discovery. We perform ablations across different values for bb: 3, 10, 25. The results are shown in Figure 21. Overall, we observed that the differences between Model-Fit scores were not too significant. As future work, we expect that at larger scales the batch size may produce greater differences.

Ablation 3: Number of Candidate Objectives For Each Batch. We as the proposer LLM to propose a fixed number of objectives for each batch. We perform ablations over this parameter: 1, 2. The results are shown in Figure 22. Overall, we observed that proposing a greater number of candidate objectives for each batch results in a higher performance. This matches our intuitions as it provides a greater search space for objectives discovery.

Ablation 4: Informative Samples Identification vs. Random. As described in Section 3.1, we sample the inputs which result in the highest average residual error, for discovery. To understand the importance of this component, we also compare it against Obj-Disco with just using random sampling. We observe these results using the misalignment case study scenario as we believe that to be the most practical setting. We observe that, out of four trials, none of the trials using random sampling discovered objectives corresponding to misalignment. In comparison, Obj-Disco (with informative sampling), discovered misalignment behavior in three out of four trials. We believe this is partially due to the residual-based sampling approach as it assists with helping discover less correlated objectives. We show all trials of the discovered objectives in Figure 23.

Ablation 5: Open-Ended Discovery vs. Fixed. We attempt to understand the importance of open-ended discovery, as described in Section 3.1, by comparing against a variation of Obj-Disco with using just a pre-defined set of objectives, which we refer to as Fixed-α\alpha, where α\alpha is the size of the pre-defined set. Details for obtaining this pre-defined set are described in Appendix A.4.1. We observe these results in terms of the case study on misalignment (Section 5.2) as we believe that to be the most practical scenario. All the qualitative results are shown in Figures 24 and 23. We find that, out of four trials, both Fixed-3 and Fixed-15 only discover misaligned objectives from one trial, whereas Obj-Disco does so in three out of four trials. We believe this helps to exhibit the importance of open-ended discovery of objectives.

A.5.2 Controlled And Open-Source Reward Model Evaluation

To rigorously evaluate Obj-Disco, we constructed synthetic ground-truth reward signals R∗R^{*} composed of linear combinations of distinct, natural language objectives. These objectives were adapted from Glaese et al. (2022) and tailored to the specific domains of our tasks. We utilized an LLM-as-a-Judge to score each response against these objectives, aggregating the scores via an equally weighted sum (13\frac{1}{3} per objective) to form the final reward signal used for alignment. Figure 26 details the specific objective definitions used for the Summarization and Multi-Turn Dialogue tasks.

For the Instruction-Following task with the Alpaca dataset, we trained our own Qwen3-4B reward model on a single dimension of a multi-objective preference dataset (Jang et al., 2023). Specifically, we used the dimension corresponding to "Choose a response that is friendly, witty, funny, and humorous, like a close friend". This allowed us to observe how similar our DIR is to a known objective on a reward model.

We show additional experimental results in Figure 25. Overall, Obj-Disco surpasses the baselines in terms of the Model-Fit score in most settings.

A.5.3 Objective Explanations Sample Results

We illustrate some sample results from our proposed Objective Explanations in Figures 27, 28, 29, 30.

A.5.4 Human-Interpretability Human-Subject User Study

We recruited 15 participants via Amazon Mechanical Turk for human evaluation of the human-interpretability of our objectives. The study interface was developed using Streamlit, with response data securely stored and managed via Supabase. We collected a total of N=400N=400 judgments. Images of the study are shown in Figures 31, 32, 33.

For the study, we provided users with an objective description, rubric, and in-context examples and asked them to score a reference model input and response, similar to how we implemented our human-interpretability verification within Obj-Disco. We note that we did not use trajectories in the user study due to the cognitive load on the Mechanical Turk users. Out of all the responses, we note that the Pearson correlation coefficient for the human and model scores was 0.497 (p-value < 0.001). Although there is room for improvement, we believe this illustrates that our human-interpretability verification does partially capture the interpretability of the objectives. We leave for future work investigation of different combinations or setups of LLM-judges to better match human oversight.

A.6 Additional Discussion

A.6.1 How To Decide The Number Of Objectives?

In practical settings, the optimal number of objectives kk is often unknown a priori. We recommend treating kk as a tunable parameter determined through an "elbow method" approach, similar to selecting the number of components in Principal Component Analysis. Specifically, developers should run Obj-Disco iteratively, monitoring the marginal decrease in Obj-Error on the validation set at each step. We suggest stopping the discovery process when the marginal improvement in the reconstruction error falls below a predefined threshold or when the newly discovered objective is semantically redundant with the existing set. This data-driven approach ensures that the discovered set R^\hat{R} is sparse yet sufficiently expressive to capture the core alignment dynamics.

What Happens If We Discover More Objectives? We show qualitative results of this scenario in Figure 34. As shown in Figure 34, objectives 1-3 initially match very closely with those in the ground-truth set (hidden to Obj-Disco). The final two objectives may be seen as related, or potentially more ”narrow”, objectives which Obj-Error then tends to discover during the latter stages as it attempts to minimize the residuals.

A.7 Limitations

Our work presents a promising approach, but it has several practical limitations. First, Obj-Disco is computationally intensive, incurring some time and financial costs (due to the LLM-as-a-Judge setup) to discover the set of objectives R^\hat{R}. In order for Obj-Disco to be feasible, our proposed method requires relatively inexpensive models, such as GPT-4o-mini to serve as the proposer and scoring models. However, such judges are also subject to inaccuracies in judgment and potential biases in their outputs, potentially skewing the results (Zheng et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2025). Furthermore, the generative nature of our objective proposer introduces stochasticity. Different runs may therefore produce varied sets of objectives, a challenge common to automated discovery methods that makes exact replication difficult (Dunlap et al., 2025). Finally, the quality of the discovered objectives may be sensitive to hyperparameter selection. For instance, the thresholds for our human-interpretability and trend-predictability criteria, ϵinterp\epsilon_{\text{interp}} and ϵtrend\epsilon_{\text{trend}}, may require careful tuning to ensure stable and meaningful results.
